\section[la angustia]{la angustia — anguish, distress}

\label{lesson:ES-C719-angustia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to joke, then the Spanish for to make fun of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la angustia}
\textbf{la angustia} — \textquotedblleft{}anguish, distress\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Sentí angustia al no tener noticias.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I felt anguish at having no news.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Me da angustia} — it makes me anxious.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{angustia} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{angustia} \textquotedblleft{}narrowness, difficulty, distress\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{angustus} \textquotedblleft{}narrow\textquotedblright{}: distress is a tightness in the chest.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la angustia}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la angustia}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la angustia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to joke, then the Spanish for to make fun of, then say \emph{la angustia} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la angustia mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Anguish, distress\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[soportar]{soportar — to bear, to put up with}

\label{lesson:ES-C719-soportar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to make fun of, then the Spanish for anguish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: soportar}
\textbf{soportar} — \textquotedblleft{}to bear, to put up with\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No soporto el ruido.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I cannot stand the noise.}
\end{quote}

\emph{No soporto a mi vecino} — I cannot stand my neighbour. A false friend: to support is \emph{apoyar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{soportar} comes from Latin \emph{supportāre} \textquotedblleft{}to carry, to convey\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{sub} \textquotedblleft{}under\textquotedblright{} and \emph{portāre} \textquotedblleft{}to carry\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{soportar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{soportar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{soportar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to make fun of, then the Spanish for anguish, then say \emph{soportar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[dudar]{dudar — to doubt}

\label{lesson:ES-C719-dudar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for anguish, then the Spanish for to bear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dudar}
\textbf{dudar} — \textquotedblleft{}to doubt\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dudo que venga hoy.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I doubt he will come today.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Dudar que} takes the subjunctive. \emph{La duda} is a doubt.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dudar} is inherited from Latin \emph{dubitāre} \textquotedblleft{}to waver, to doubt\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); the middle \emph{-bit-} wore away.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dudar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dudar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{dudar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for anguish, then the Spanish for to bear, then say \emph{dudar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does dudar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To doubt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la preocupación]{la preocupación — worry, concern}

\label{lesson:ES-C719-preocupacion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to bear, then the Spanish for to doubt.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la preocupación}
\textbf{la preocupación} — \textquotedblleft{}worry, concern\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi mayor preocupación es la salud.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My biggest worry is health.}
\end{quote}

The verb \emph{preocuparse} is to worry.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{preocupación} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{praeoccupātiō} \textquotedblleft{}a seizing beforehand\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); a worry takes hold of the mind before anything else can.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la preocupación}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la preocupación}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to bear, then the Spanish for to doubt, then say \emph{la preocupación} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la preocupación mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Worry, concern\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[preocupado]{preocupado — worried}

\label{lesson:ES-C719-preocupado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to doubt, then the Spanish for worry.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: preocupado}
\textbf{preocupado} — \textquotedblleft{}worried\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Estoy preocupado por mi padre.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am worried about my father.}
\end{quote}

Used with \emph{estar}: \emph{estar preocupado por}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{preocupado} is the participle of \emph{preocupar}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{praeoccupāre} \textquotedblleft{}to seize beforehand\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{occupāre} \textquotedblleft{}to seize\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{preocupado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to doubt, then the Spanish for worry, then say \emph{preocupado} again
